title: Platform Economics & Trust Playbook for Architects
author: Priya Mehta
body:
Purpose and scope:
This playbook is a compact, field-ready guide intended for platform engineering teams, security architects, and procurement partners who must evaluate LLM inference choices under three constraints: predictable economics, operational trust, and fast time-to-value. It combines concise positioning, a competitor-focused economics brief, a 10-slide pitch outline, concrete pricing scenarios, two succinct case studies, a prospect-friendly Security FAQ, and a recommended 6-week pilot template.

Executive summary (one paragraph):
Platform teams choosing Redwood Inference get a single runtime abstraction across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments that reduces integration surface area, exposes cost levers (batching, KV prefix caching, quantization), and provides enterprise-grade controls (KMS/HSM integration, request audit logs, RBAC). The outcome for customers is lower and more predictable unit cost, fewer operational incidents during rollouts, and a compliance posture suitable for regulated workloads.

Target audiences and decision makers:
- Platform engineering lead / head of platform
- Cloud architects and SRE leads
- CISO / security & tech risk
- Procurement and vendor selection committees

Core positioning statements (short bullets to use in briefing decks):
- For platform engineers: "One API to serve everywhere — identical operational model across hosted, reserved, and private deployments."
- For finance/procurement: "Transparent per-1k-token economics and reserve options that smooth monthly spend volatility."
- For security teams: "Private deployment options and customer-managed key integration for data and key sovereignty."

Competitive economics brief (practical takeaways):
- Competitor buckets: public cloud managed endpoints, API-first LLM providers, and self-hosted runtimes.
- Key differentiators vs each:
  * Public cloud endpoints: better ecosystem but limited token-level controls and generally higher egress/operational cost for sustained inference.
  * API-first vendors: usually fastest to integrate; fewer enterprise controls (on-prem, HSM) and limited SLAs.
  * Self-hosted/runtime builds: maximum control but highest ops burden and slower time-to-production.
- Compelling field claim: Redwood reduces operational integration time compared with self-hosting, and reduces sustained per-token cost vs cloud endpoints by making batching, caching, and quantization practical and observable.

10-slide pitch deck (fieldable, with slide guidance):
1) Cover: audience, use case, one-line outcome (tailor to platform/security/procurement)
2) Problem: fragmentation between model ownership and serving reliability/economics
3) Outcome snapshot: latency, cost, reliability improvements from customers
4) Product modes: Hosted / Dedicated / Private (one-liner each)
5) How it works (high level): routing, KV cache, batching, quantization, rollout policies
6) Economics worked example (summary table)
7) Security & controls: KMS, audit logs, RBAC, data residency options
8) Migration path: trial -> pilot -> reserved commit -> enterprise private
9) Case studies: two one-paragraph callouts (see case study section)
10) Ask & next steps: pilot scope, metrics, timeline, contact

Field presentation tips (two-liners):
- Start with slide 6 for procurement-heavy audiences; dive into slide 7 for CISOs; for platform teams expand slide 5 into a technical session.
- Always carry a priced pilot worksheet (see appendix link) with per-route assumptions.

Pricing guidance and worked scenarios (practical rules of thumb):
Principles to follow when proposing pricing:
- Anchor conversations on per-1k-token economics and total service cost (tokens + reserved pool amortized fees + egress + retention).
- Offer three entry motions: trial (metered hosted), reserved capacity (monthly commit + lower unit fee), private (license + support + optional capacity).
- Use commit discounts to lock predictable high-utilization flows; preserve higher short-term unit fees for bursty traffic.

Scenario 1: Customer support assistant (midmarket SaaS)
- Traffic: 80k monthly queries, avg 600 tokens/request
- Incumbent cloud endpoint (public): approx $0.07 per 1k tokens -> monthly cost ~ $3,360
- Redwood hosted (with batching & caching layer): estimate $0.028 per 1k tokens -> monthly cost ~ $1,344 (approx 60% reduction)
- Reserved capacity (12mo) example: pool cost $5,500/mo + $0.008 per 1k tokens -> net monthly ~ $2,224; breakeven vs incumbent at sustained growth above ~115k queries/month

Scenario 2: Regulated health product (private deployment)
- One-time deployment & services: $120,000 (installation, network integration, validation)
- Annual support & licensing: 15% of license in year 1.
- First-year fully-burdened cost depends on consolidation: multiple product lines > 2x consolidation typically yields ROI in year 1.

Discount and concession guidance (sales play):
- Typical reserved-commit discounts: 10-30% (scale with term and committed throughput).
- Professional services: price as T&M or fixed milestone, include a 10% contingency for network/security complexity.
- Preserve observability add-ons (longer retention, premium SLAs) as margin-preserving concessions.

Pilot template (recommended 6-week structure):
Week 0: Kickoff & metrics definition (traffic slice, latency targets, eval prompts)
Weeks 1-3: Integration, smoke tests, initial telemetry (route 5-10% of traffic)
Week 4: Capacity tuning (batching, cache policies, quantization profile) and cost run-rate update
Week 5: Security validation (audit log inspection, pen test scope)
Week 6: Decision review (go/no-go; convert to reserved or extend pilot)
Success metrics (suggested):
- Latency: 95th percentile below agreed SLO (e.g., 300ms for short-text generation)
- Cost: >= 40% reduction in per-token unit cost vs incumbent (pilot subset)
- Quality: no regression on agreed prompt evals (50-prompt set; mean preference score unchanged or improved)

Two condensed case studies (one-paragraph each):
- Case study A: FinOps analytics platform (midmarket). Problem: high recurring cost for embeddings and summarization across product modules. Action: Routed embeddings and short summarization requests to Redwood hosted, tuned batching and introduced KV prefix caching for repeated context. Outcome: 56% token-cost reduction and a 70% drop in inference-related operational incidents during model rollouts. Pilot moved to a 12-month reserved commit in 9 weeks.
- Case study B: Clinical workflow platform (regulated). Problem: required inference inside customer VPC with HSM-backed KMS and strict audit retention. Action: Deployed Redwood Private with customer-managed KMS, performed SOC2 evidence exchange and audit log validation. Outcome: Private deployment completed in 14 weeks, met the provider's compliance gates and consolidated inference workloads across three product lines; net first-year ROI estimated at ~1.4x after consolidation.

Security & compliance FAQ (prospect-friendly):
Q: Where is data stored and how long is it retained?
A: Data for Hosted customers is encrypted in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest; retention windows are configurable per-route. Dedicated and Private deployments can be configured to honor customer retention policies and store logs in customer-managed buckets when required.

Q: Can we use our KMS/HSM?
A: Yes. Dedicated and Private deployments support customer-managed KMS; Private on-prem installs can integrate with customer HSM for key storage and signing operations.

Q: Do you provide request-level audit logs and request tracing?
A: Yes. Audit logs (request metadata, model version, route id) are supported for Dedicated and Private customers and retention is configurable to meet compliance needs.

Q: Which compliance artifacts do you provide?
A: We provide SOC 2 Type II reports and an enterprise security evidence binder. We can provide ISO guidance artifacts and a GDPR data residency playbook on request.

Q: How are model artifacts protected?
A: Model artifacts run in isolated runtime namespaces. For Private installs, artifacts and model weights can be stored on customer-managed storage. Access to artifacts is governed by RBAC and SSO integration.

Operational readiness checklist (for platform teams):
- Network: VPC planning (ingress/egress), private endpoints, routing policies
- IAM: RBAC mapping (admin/operator/viewer), SSO integration test
- Observability: enable token-level telemetry, per-route dashboards, alerts for latency & error rate
- Recovery: snapshot model configs and rollout policies prior to canary

Negotiation and conversion play tips for field teams (practical):
- Offer a scoped pilot with explicit conversion criteria tied to unit economics (e.g., X% cost reduction on pilot subset within 6 weeks).
- Trade longer-term commit for lower unit fees and staged reductions at 6/12/24 months rather than one-off deep discounts.
- Bundle observability retention and premium SLAs as add-ons to preserve margin while meeting procurement asks.

Appendix: quick CLI example for trial call (curl) and sample response (illustrative):
- Example request: curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"rwd/lite-7b","input":"Summarize the following...","max_tokens":256}'
- Example response (illustrative): {"request_id":"req_abc123","model":"rwd/lite-7b","latency_ms":95,"tokens_consumed":210,"output":"..."}
